claim: appeal against sentence
requested_remedy: appeal against sentence

facts.F1: The Appellant, So Oi Ying, was convicted after trial of an offence of conspiracy to steal and sentenced to a term of 18 months imprisonment.
facts.F2: The Appellant appealed against the sentence.
facts.F3: The Appellant was one of 4 defendants (D1-D4) initially charged with theft and receiving stolen goods.
facts.F4: The prosecution alleged that the 4 defendants were a gang operating together in a shop lifting spree.
facts.F5: D1 pleaded guilty and was sentenced to a term of 12 months imprisonment.
facts.F6: D3 pleaded guilty and was sentenced to a term of 8 months imprisonment.
facts.F7: D2 was convicted after trial and sentenced to a term of 12 months imprisonment.
facts.F8: The learned Magistrate amended the charge against the Appellant to conspiracy to steal, following the close of the prosecution case, under Section 27 of the Magistrates Ordinance.
facts.F9: The Appellant's conviction for conspiracy to steal was not appealed against.
facts.F10: The Magistrate sentenced the Appellant to 18 months' imprisonment, taking into account her full involvement in the gang's activities and her previous convictions for theft in Hong Kong in 1998.
facts.F11: The Appellant had no discount applied to her sentence, unlike her co-defendants who had pleaded guilty and received a one-third discount.
facts.F12: The Appellant might have misunderstood the position given the sole charge upon which the prosecution had relied up to the close of its case.

reference_issues: Whether the Appellant's sentence was manifestly excessive compared to her co-defendants.
Whether the Appellant was prejudiced by the prosecution's amendment of the charge to conspiracy to steal.

facts.F2: The Plaintiff, the IO, comprises 2 residential blocks with shops on the ground and first floor and residential units on the 2nd to 25th floors.
facts.F3: The IO brought this action to recover Sam Woo's share of contribution to the costs for the repair and renovation works of the Building.
facts.F4: The Building is subject to a Deed of Mutual Covenants (DMC) dated 18 January 1983.
facts.F5: Sam Woo became the owner of the Shop on 18 June 1992.
facts.F6: The IO held an owners' meeting on 17 January 2008 to discuss a repair and renovation project.
facts.F7: Various repair and renovation works were approved, and a resolution was passed for the repair and renovation charges (the Charges) to be contributed by owners.
facts.F8: Sam Woo took out an application at the Lands Tribunal to determine its share of the Charges, which was ruled to be calculated in accordance with its undivided shares of the Building, i.e. 963/14,922.

facts.F10: The IO issued a demand notice to Sam Woo for the sum of HK$211,407.00 on 14 May 2010.
facts.F11: Sam Woo agreed to the amount but contended that there was a total over-payment of HK$272,100.00 over the years and hence was not liable for further contribution.
facts.F12: The amounts paid by Sam Woo were part of the monthly management charges that had not yet been used by the IO.

facts.F14: The resolutions passed at the owners' meeting were valid and did not conflict with Clause 3(i) of the DMC

claim: The plaintiff sought leave to appeal from an arbitration award under section 23 of the Arbitration Ordinance.
requested_remedy: The plaintiff sought leave to appeal from an arbitration award under section 23 of the Arbitration Ordinance.
parties: Plaintiff: China Link Construction Company Limited

facts.F1: A fire broke out at the basement level of a building project known as Hok Un Redevelopment Phase I on 12 September 1996.
facts.F2: The plaintiff, a subcontractor, became entitled to claim under an All Risks policy issued by the defendant.
facts.F3: Disputes between the plaintiff and the defendant were referred to arbitration, and Ms Teresa Cheng, SC, was appointed as sole arbitrator on 11 December 1998.
facts.F4: The substantive hearing of the arbitration took place in June and July 2000 and lasted eight days.
facts.F5: The Arbitrator published an Interim Award on 4 May 2001, dismissing the plaintiff's claim and leaving only the question of costs outstanding.
facts.F6: The plaintiff issued a Notice of Originating Motion on 25 May 2001, which was the last day for service under section 23(2) of the Ordinance.
facts.F7: The plaintiff's solicitors wrote to the defendant's solicitors on 15 June 2001, suggesting that the substantive application for the appeal be heard immediately after the application for leave to appeal.
facts.F8: The defendant's solicitors rejected this suggestion on 27 June 2001.
facts.F9: The plaintiff's solicitors wrote to the court on 13 July 2001, seeking an appointment to fix a one-day hearing for the originating motion, which was never held.
facts.F10: The plaintiff's solicitors cancelled the appointment, with the consent of the defendant, after indicating that the plaintiff would serve its affidavit evidence by 31 July 2001.
facts.F11: The plaintiff failed to serve its affidavit evidence by 31 July 2001.
facts.F12: The defendant's solicitors wrote to the Arbitrator on 1 June 2001, requesting an order for costs in the defendant's favour.
facts.F13: The plaintiff's solicitors responded on 15 June 2001, stating that the question of costs should be determined after the resolution of the application for leave to appeal.
facts.F14: The Arbitrator gave directions for the resolution of the question of costs on 2 November 2001.
facts.F15: The defendant's solicitors sent a letter to the plaintiff's solicitors on 15 November 2001, stating that the plaintiff had failed to progress its application for leave to appeal and that the delay was grossly excessive.
facts.F16: The plaintiff's solicitors responded on 27 October 2001, stating that further time was required to serve the affidavit in relation to the appeal.
facts.F17: The plaintiff served its affidavit evidence on 12 January 2002, 7.5 months after the Notice of Originating Motion was issued.
facts.F18: The defendant applied to strike out the Notice of Originating Summons for want of prosecution on 14 December 2001.
facts.F19: No justification was provided by the plaintiff for the delay in prosecuting its application for leave to appeal.

facts.F1: The Appellant, a 19 year old male, was convicted of a single charge of indecent assault after trial by a deputy Magistrate.

facts.F3: The Appellant gave evidence on the special issue as did his mother.

facts.F5: On the general issue the Appellant gave evidence as did a government psychiatrist, Dr Mo, whom he had commenced consulting in August 2004.
facts.F6: Dr Mo is attached to North District Hospital.
facts.F7: In addition, the report of a private psychiatrist, a Dr Chan, was referred to by Dr Mo:  the Appellant had commenced consulting Dr Chan on the 22nd April 2004.
facts.F8: His report was substantially more detailed than that of Dr Mo in regard to the Appellant’s background, his behaviour and his personal circumstances in the years preceding the offence as related to him by the Appellant and his mother.
facts.F9: Dr Chan was not called as a witness.
facts.F10: Dr Mo had prepared a report in advance of the hearing.
facts.F11: Prior to giving evidence she was afforded access to Dr Chan’s report in which he expressed the view that: “The present alleged offence was more likely to be due to his psychotic illness than genuine sexual intention to assault the victim indecently”
facts.F12: Once she was in possession of the additional information contained in Dr Chan’s report, Dr Mo expressed herself in agreement with this conclusion.
facts.F13: The Magistrate rejected Dr Mo’s opinion and, effectively, the opinion of Dr Chan which Dr Mo adopted.
facts.F14: The fact that a witness is called as an expert does not confer upon his evidence, especially opinions which he may offer, any enhanced status.
facts.F15: Evidence of an expert may be rejected even where it is unchallenged.
facts.F16: But the reasons for doing so must be sound.
facts.F17: The assault itself occurred in this manner:  the Appellant had been walking towards the complainant across a footbridge:  he walked past her and she felt the flat of a hand touch her left breast for some one to two seconds.
facts.F18: She looked at the Appellant who, in turn, was looking at her:  he then withdrew his hand and smiled at her with what was described as “an indecent smile”.
facts.F19: The complainant at that stage, according to the Magistrate, did not think that the Appellant was “suffering from any mental disease”.
facts.F20: The Magistrate categorised the evidence of the police officer who arrested the Appellant as being to the effect that he “did not have the impression that the [Appellant] was suffering from any mental illness”
facts.F21: The Magistrate does not indicate the basis of the opinions of these two witnesses nor does she indicate whether either of them had any expertise in assessing whether persons are suffering from mental illness or not.
facts.F22: The Magistrate also made reference to the facial expression of the Appellant as related by these two witnesses to further support her rejection of the psychiatric evidence.
facts.F23: She says: “So the [Appellant’s] appearance was in direct contradiction to the appearance of a person suffering from long time psychiatric illness without treatment as described by Dr. Mo.”

claim: speeding, contrary to section 41(1)(a) of the Road Traffic Ordinance, Cap. 374
requested_remedy: speeding, contrary to section 41(1)(a) of the Road Traffic Ordinance, Cap. 374
parties: Defendant: LAU KWOK FAI BERNARD (劉國輝)

facts.F1: The appellant was convicted of one count of “speeding”, contrary to section 41(1)(a) of the Road Traffic Ordinance, Cap. 374.
facts.F2: The summons alleged that the appellant drove a private car displaying registration mark GY6986 on a road at a speed of 66 kilometres per hour, which exceeded 50 kilometres per hour being the speed limit then in force on that road.
facts.F3: PW2, a police officer, monitored the speed of vehicles passing the relevant section of the road with the help of a laser gun and found that the appellant was driving at 70 km/h.
facts.F4: The summons stated that the appellant was driving at 66 km/h because the police normally deduct 4 km/h from laser gun readings.
facts.F5: The police would take no action against vehicles travelling under 63 km/h, but would issue penalty tickets to vehicles travelling in excess of 64 km/h (50 km/h plus an allowance of 14 km/h).
facts.F6: PW1, an expert from a laser gun factory, said that the laser gun in question has “an allowance of plus and minus 2 kilometres”.
facts.F7: The Traffic Procedures Manual (TPM) states that the lowest enforcement level of a section of a road with a speed limit of 50 km/h is 57 km/h.
facts.F8: The appellant elected not to give evidence but raised an argument that the prosecution should have deducted 7 kilometres instead of 4 kilometres from the laser gun reading.
facts.F9: The TPM provides for two allowances: the “lowest enforcement level” and the “technical allowance”.
facts.F10: The upward and downward adjustments under paragraphs 2(a) and 2(c) of the TPM provide two allowances, which go far more than making up for the slight deviation of plus and minus 2 kilometres produced by the laser gun.

reference_issues: Whether the prosecution should have deducted 7 kilometres instead of 4 kilometres from the laser gun reading
Whether the Traffic Procedures Manual (TPM) provides for a lowest enforcement level of 57 km/h for a section of a road with a speed limit of 50 km/h

Traffic Procedures Manual (TPM)
